endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: A cutoff was established via discussions with clinicians, so the output value is shown as either high or low risk rather than a value between 0 and 1

endorsements.title: Machine learning models in clinical practice for the prediction of postoperative complications after major abdominal surgery
endorsements.quote: When risk scores are created, it is essential that several experts in the field of surgery, nursery, or data science discuss the favorable cut-off values together.

endorsements.title: A roadmap to implementing machine learning in healthcare: from concept to practice
endorsements.quote: For PREDICT use cases, operational performance data at multiple thresholds are presented to the clinical team, who can choose a threshold value based on both predictive performance and operational feasibility.

evidence.title: The effect of computerised decision support alerts tailored to intensive care on the administration of high-risk drug combinations, and their monitoring: a cluster randomised stepped-wedge trial
evidence.outcome: Administered high-risk drug combinations per 1000 drug administrations per patient
evidence.effect: Mean 26·2 (SD 53·4) intervention vs 35·6 (65·0) control; 12% decrease (95% CI 5-18%; p=0·0008) after adjustment for clustering and prognostic factors.
evidence.quote: Tailoring potential DDI alerts to the ICU led to a 12% decrease (95% CI 5-18%; p=0·0008) in the number of administered high-risk drug combinations per 1000 drug administrations per patient, after adjusting for clustering and prognostic factors.

evidence.title: Prospective implementation of AI-assisted screen reading to improve early detection of breast cancer
evidence.outcome: Proportion of cases flagged for review and additional cancers detected after threshold adjustment
evidence.effect: Threshold moved to a more specific point for workload capacity: flagged cases fell from 10.6–11.2% (pilots) to 7.4% live, CDR still +0.7/1,000. Simulated higher-specificity point flagged 2.9% while detecting 10 of 11 additional cancers.
evidence.quote: Before launching the AI system into live use, its decision threshold was adjusted to a more specific predetermined operating point to accommodate the site’s workload capacity, resulting in a smaller proportion of cases (7.4%, 1,186/15,953) flagged for additional review in live use.

evidence.title: Clinical implementation of an AI-enabled ECG for hypertrophic cardiomyopathy detection
evidence.outcome: Alert percentage and enrolment rate after algorithm operating-point optimisation
evidence.effect: Alert percentage decreased from 4.4% (2097/47868) to 2.3% (2251/97980), p<0.0001, with no difference in the enrolment rate by alerts reviewed.
evidence.quote: During the study, deployment of an optimised algorithm operating point helped reduce the alert percentage of algorithm-screened patients from 4.4% (2097/47868) to 2.3% (2251/97980), p<0.0001, with no difference in the enrolment rate by alerts reviewed.

evidence.title: DeepCARS-Identified High-Risk Patients: Clinical Interventions and Outcomes During the Korean Healthcare Crisis
evidence.outcome: Alternative alert cutoff's discrimination for physician active intervention
evidence.effect: ROC analysis suggested a cutoff of ≥94 (rather than ≥91) for better intervention discrimination (AUC = 0.708); DeepCARS ≥94 independently predicted active intervention (OR 3.52).
evidence.quote: ROC analysis suggested a cutoff of ≥94 for better intervention discrimination (AUC = 0.708).
evidence.sample_unit: adult ward patients with DeepCARS alerts

evidence.title: Beyond the Model: Practical Insights from Monitoring Predictive Models across Diverse Clinical Workflows
evidence.outcome: Alignment of preimplementation thresholds with clinical capacity and workflows
evidence.effect: Silent alert simulations supported threshold selection aligned with clinical capacity and workflows. Their ability to predict postimplementation performance was limited; no quantitative results were reported.
evidence.quote: Silent alert simulations proved valuable for selecting preimplementation thresholds that aligned with clinical capacity and workflows but were limited in predicting postimplementation performance when the models faced real-world human-alert interactions.

evidence.title: Prospective validation and implementation of a model to identify patients with carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) carriage on admission to acute care hospitals
evidence.outcome: resource and predictive yield trade-offs
evidence.effect: Raising the threshold to 0.36% would reduce screening volume to 5 patients per week and increase PPV to 19%, while minimally reducing NPV.
evidence.quote: For example, using a higher cutoff (≥0.36%) may be more practical as it would require screening fewer patients (∼5/week) with a higher PPV (19%), while only sacrificing a small decrease in NPV (98.2% to 97.5%).

evidence.title: Optimizing the Implementation of Clinical Predictive Models to Minimize National Costs: Sepsis Case Study
evidence.outcome: Cost savings and DOR when alert cutoffs are chosen accounting for false alarm tolerance and department incidence
evidence.effect: Department-specific optimized thresholds raised DOR by up to 50 versus uniform recommended threshold (DOR up to 116) and increased savings; simulated only, no clinician input tested.
evidence.quote: Figure 5 D shows that DOR can increase by as much as 50 when switching from a uniform recommended threshold to heterogeneous thresholds, even though DOR is not directly maximized.

evidence.title: Economic evaluation for medical artificial intelligence: accuracy vs. cost-effectiveness in a diabetic retinopathy screening case
evidence.outcome: Optimal AI cutoff selection accounting for prevalence, willingness-to-pay/resource capacity
evidence.effect: Optimal sensitivity/specificity varied by prevalence and WTP; at WTP over US$5000 sensitivity should exceed specificity; lower WTP favored lower sensitivity/higher specificity.
evidence.quote: Specifically, in settings with WTP levels over US$ 5000, sensitivity should always be higher than specificity for cost-effective consideration.
evidence.sample_unit: participants with diabetes (simulated cohort; 1100 sensitivity/specificity scenarios)

evidence.title: Preparing for the bedside-optimizing a postpartum depression risk prediction model for clinical implementation in a health system
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Threshold selection using decision curve net benefit, sensitivity, and positive prediction rates
evidence.effect: Net benefit was highest at 0.3-0.4 thresholds; 0.2 predicted 19-23% positive versus 13-18% at 0.3 and 11-15% at 0.4; threshold 0.3 balanced true and false positives while 0.2 missed fewer at-risk patients.
evidence.quote: A threshold of 0.3 produces positive predictions that are close to the observed prevalence at the AMC, while a threshold of 0.2 generates more positive predictions potentially allowing us to capture more at-risk patients albeit with false positive predictions.

evidence.title: Optimizing Artificial Intelligence Thresholds for Mammographic Lesion Detection: A Retrospective Study on Diagnostic Performance and Radiologist-Artificial Intelligence Discordance
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity and specificity of category-specific versus single AI cutoffs
evidence.effect: Youden-optimal thresholds were 19 (4A; sens 0.71, spec 0.64) and 63 (4B/4C; sens 0.82, spec 0.92); a single threshold of 35 cut 4A sensitivity to 41.2%. Thresholds were not selected with clinician input or response capacity.
evidence.quote: These findings suggest that separate thresholds for different BI-RADS categories are necessary to avoid missing cancers in the BI-RADS 4A group.

evidence.title: Automated Scan Region Classification and Patient-specific Dose Modeling for Enhanced Dose Management in Computed Tomography
evidence.outcome: Number of cases flagged for review by patient-specific outlier method versus fixed DRL exceedances
evidence.effect: Patient-specific models flagged 60 statistical outliers versus 170 DRL exceedances; all flagged cases manually confirmed as clinically justified.
evidence.quote: Crucially, the patient-specific models identified substantially fewer cases for review (60 statistical outliers) compared with the standard DRL-based method (170 exceedances).

evidence.title: How threshold customisation affects the performance of a multiclass X-ray AI model for primary care triage: a retrospective study
evidence.outcome: Threshold selection with clinician input balancing operational value and false negatives
evidence.effect: Threshold 0.1 chosen collaboratively with physicians and radiologists; sensitivity 93.19%, operational improvement 35.85% retained.
evidence.quote: Hence, the 0.1 threshold was deemed to have an acceptable sensitivity for safety and still retain acceptable potential operational improvement to yield value in implementation.

evidence.title: Decision Curve Analysis for Evaluating Machine Learning Models for Next-Day Transfer Out of ICU
evidence.outcome: Threshold selection aligned with workflow capacity (8 hour daily review time constraint)
evidence.effect: At a feasible operating threshold (0.23), the model flagged ~23 charts/day and yielded ~1.23 enrollments/day under conservative eligibility and consent assumptions.
evidence.quote: At a feasible operating threshold (0.23), the model flagged ∼23 charts/day and yielded ∼1.23 enrollments/day under conservative eligibility and consent assumptions.

evidence.title: Alert Policy and Rare-Event Metrics for Seven-Day-Ahead Agitation Forecasting in Passive Dementia Monitoring
evidence.outcome: Precision, recall and alert burden at default versus F1-optimized thresholds
evidence.effect: Default thresholds gave 20–23% precision with 94–100% recall; optimized thresholds raised precision to 73–82% with 56.25% recall, cutting expected false alarms by more than half.
evidence.quote: Default thresholds yielded 20–23% precision with 94– 100% recall—unacceptable for caregiver-facing alerts.

evidence.title: Integrating Clinical Priorities into the Technical Validation of Machine Learning Classifiers: A Generalizable Framework Demonstrated on Opioid Misuse Screening
evidence.outcome: Effect of decision threshold choice on sensitivity, false positives, and net benefit
evidence.effect: Lowering threshold to 0.33 raised sensitivity from 38.5% to 51.3% and false positives from 119 to 207, reducing PPV from 42.2% to 35.9%; model preference shifted with cost ratio (crossover c_FN≈3.03).
evidence.quote: The threshold reduction that increased CSBT-Tuned sensitivity from 38.5% to 51.3% simultaneously increased false positives from 119 to 207, reducing PPV from 42.2% to 35.9%.
evidence.sample_unit: survey respondents in the held-out test set (NSDUH 2015-2019)

evidence.title: Identifying risk factors for drug use recurrence with ecological momentary assessment, wearable technologies, and machine learning: a feasibility trial of peer recovery support specialist intervention
evidence.outcome: Staff burden from responding to algorithm-generated alerts
evidence.effect: PRSS made 483 call attempts, ~20 per participant (range 1-53), ~21 calls/week; only 36% of first calls answered; burden on PRSS described as high.
evidence.quote: Important aspects related to feasibility included difficulties with learning how to use the RNI Health app, the high burden of daily entries with the RNI Health app, limited battery life of the wearable devices, loss of wearable devices, and the high burden of responding by phone to numerous alerts generated by the algorithms.

evidence.title: Multicenter Prospective Validation of an Updated Proprietary Sepsis Prediction Model
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value and alert burden of sepsis model alerts
evidence.effect: PPV was low, 0.13 (95% CI, 0.13-0.14) to 0.26 (95% CI, 0.25-0.27), with a high number needed to evaluate and high alert burden.
evidence.quote: Positive predictive values remained low, from 0.13 (95% CI, 0.13-0.14) to 0.26 (95% CI, 0.25-0.27), with a high number needed to evaluate and high alert burden.

evidence.title: Real-time Inflammation Panel for inpatient care: a before-after evaluation of post-analytic timeliness and outcomes at a tertiary center
evidence.outcome: Alert burden per patient-day after deployment of rule-based alerts
evidence.effect: Alert burden averaged 0.23 alerts/patient-day with around 4% duplicate suppression; sensitivity 0.88 and PPV 0.83 against an operational composite.
evidence.quote: Alert burden averaged 0.23 alerts/patient-day with around 4% duplicate suppression.

evidence.title: Don’t set and forget: Optimising Digital Early Warning Tools through upgrade and evaluation
evidence.outcome: Alert fatigue reported by clinicians
evidence.effect: Stakeholders reported issues with alert fatigue from the early warning tool.
evidence.quote: Stakeholder focus groups and surveys identified a lack of awareness of specific functionality, issues with alert fatigue, technical challenges with the system, the need for training and concerns around over-reliance on the system by junior staff.

evidence.title: SURPASS-HF: Safety and Utility of Remote Pulmonary Artery Sensor Shared-management in Heart Failure
evidence.outcome: Provider alert burden and resolution from AI-supported PA-pressure threshold alerts
evidence.effect: 53 provider alerts (0.88/patient-month), all resolved (median 24 h), no overrides; 17 of 19 per-protocol patients (89%) needed no escalation.
evidence.quote: TIR-PAP was 88.4% (ITT)/91.3% (PP); reading adherence 92.1%; 53 provider alerts (0.88/patient-month) all resolved (median 24 h) with no overrides.

evidence.title: Sepsis Prediction in Hospitalized Children: Clinical Decision Support Design and Deployment
evidence.outcome: Alert burden of sepsis prediction alerts per non-ICU patient days after deployment
evidence.effect: 264 alerts on 173 patients; 10 alerts per 1000 non-ICU patient days per month; 89% bedside huddle completion; no special cause variation in days between sepsis-attributable emergent transfers.
evidence.quote: An automated electronic health record-based sepsis prediction model, CDS tools, and sepsis huddle workflows were implemented on inpatient units with a relatively low rate of interruptive alerts and high compliance with bedside huddles.

evidence.title: Ability of machine-learning based clinical decision support system to reduce alert fatigue, wrong-drug errors, and alert users about look alike, sound alike medication
evidence.venue: Computer methods and programs in biomedicine
evidence.outcome: Alert rate and acceptance rate of ML-based medication alerts in outpatient prescribing
evidence.effect: 28,536 alerts across 1,206,895 prescriptions (2.36% alert rate); 13,947 (48.88%) accepted; 470 intercepted errors (1.64% of alerts).
evidence.quote: Over the two-year study period, 1,206,895 prescriptions were ordered and a total of 28,536 alerts were triggered (alert rate: 2.36 %).

evidence.title: Development and Implementation of a Clinical Decision Support System to Enhance Efficiency and Accuracy in Medication Prescription Review in a Tertiary Care Hospital: A Retrospective Hospital CDSS Register Study
evidence.outcome: Medication alert rate and proportion of patients receiving alerts before vs after CDSS implementation
evidence.effect: Alert rate fell from 2.52% to 2.30% of orders; patients receiving alerts fell from 30.34% to 28.08%. Across 115 wards, 45.22% had fewer patients alerted and 20.87% had more.
evidence.quote: Among these, 130,286 (2.52%) and 133,562 (2.30%) prescriptions triggered alerts, indicating a significant reduction in the alert rate of 0.22%

evidence.title: Real-World Artificial Intelligence-Based Electrocardiographic Analysis to Diagnose Hypertrophic Cardiomyopathy
evidence.outcome: False positive flags and sensitivity/PPV tradeoff across probability thresholds
evidence.effect: Of 1,265 flagged patients, 691 (54.6%) had alternate diagnosis; PPV highest (66%) at ≥0.95 but sensitivity 50%; ≥0.85 gave 95% sensitivity.
evidence.quote: The positive predictive value was the highest (66%) at the cutoff ≥0.95 but with a lower sensitivity at 50%.

evidence.title: Increasing Advance Care Planning Discussions and Documentation
evidence.venue: Journal of the advanced practitioner in oncology
evidence.outcome: insufficient patient flagging
evidence.effect: The model initially flagged fewer patients than expected for increased mortality risk, prompting a threshold adjustment to include medium-risk patients.
evidence.quote: Fewer patients than expected were flagged as being at increased risk of mortality. Therefore, in July 2022, the prediction model was adjusted to include patients at medium risk of mortality, in addition to high and critical risk.

evidence.title: Performance of a Sepsis Prediction Model Across Different Sepsis Definitions
evidence.outcome: Positive predictive value and lead time at model score thresholds (alert burden from false positives)
evidence.effect: At the Sepsis-3 Youden threshold (score 9), PPV was 11.4% with median lead time 3.4 h; PPV was 6.8% for SEP-1 and 5.9% for ASE. AUPRC was 0.11-0.24.
evidence.quote: Although the model provided some advance warning before sepsis onset, a high false-positive rate may limit its clinical utility without careful threshold selection and tailored implementation.

evidence.title: Governing Decisions of Probability Cutoffs in Clinical AI Deployment: A Case Study of Asthma Exacerbation Prediction
evidence.outcome: alert volume and missed-event trade-offs
evidence.effect: Statistically optimal thresholds may produce operationally infeasible alert volumes or unacceptable miss rates.
evidence.quote: We demonstrate that statistically optimal thresholds may produce operationally infeasible alert volumes or unacceptable miss rates.

evidence.title: AI-clinician collaboration via disagreement prediction: A decision pipeline and retrospective analysis of real-world radiologist-AI interactions
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity of clinician burden to disagreement-model false positive rate (operating point)
evidence.effect: An FPR of 0.01 gives 9.55% ± 0.06% burden reduction, whereas an FPR of 0.10 gives a 12.04% ± 0.09% increase.
evidence.quote: Although an FPR of 0.01 can result in an expected 9.55% ± 0.06% reduction in burden, an FPR of 0.10 actually results in a 12.04% ± 0.09% increase.

evidence.title: Potential impact of a new sepsis prediction model for the primary care setting: early health economic evaluation using an observational cohort
evidence.outcome: Referral and mortality effects of different risk cut-offs
evidence.effect: Low cut-offs (2, 3) increased unnecessary referrals (85%, 56% vs 15% observed); cut-off 4 lowered sepsis referral to 60% and raised estimated sepsis mortality (18 vs 9 cases).
evidence.quote: At higher prediction model cut-offs (scores 3 and 4), sepsis mortality will increase according to the expert opinion analysis.

evidence.title: Development and external validation of the eFalls tool: a multivariable prediction model for the risk of ED attendance or hospitalisation with a fall or fracture in older adults
evidence.outcome: Net benefit at clinician-specified risk thresholds (10-25%) on external validation
evidence.effect: Model was no better than treat-none in the prespecified 10-25% range before recalibration; after recalibration superior for thresholds up to 18%.
evidence.quote: Decision curves show that the eFalls model had clinical utility at lower threshold probabilities on external validation, but was no better than the treat-none alternative in the pre-specified range of 10–25%.

evidence.title: Efficacy of Early Warning Scores as the Prediction Tool for Detecting Patients With Acute Deterioration in a High Dependent Unit
evidence.outcome: Whether default risk cutoffs identify high-risk patients
evidence.effect: Lowering VSI threshold to ≥1.5 raised identification of patients with outcomes from 36% to 84% about two hours before the first outcome; NEWS optimal threshold 6.0-8.0.
evidence.quote: From time trend analysis, lowering the threshold to VSI≧1.5 for high-risk led to a significant increase in the identification of patients with outcomes from 36% to 84% at about two hours before the first outcome (Figure 4 ).

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-powered tiered early warning framework addressing high false alarm rates for in-hospital mortality prediction
evidence.outcome: positive predictive value and false positive burden at standard decision thresholds
evidence.effect: PPVs remained low at 13.9% in H1, 11.0% in H2, and 9.8% in H3 under Youden index thresholds, revealing a high false positive alert burden under realistic deployment conditions.
evidence.quote: However, PPVs remained low (13.9% in H1, 11.0% in H2, and 9.8% in H3), revealing a high false positive burden under realistic deployment conditions.

evidence.title: Combining Machine Learning Models and Screening to Enhance Suicide Risk Identification for American Indian Patients: Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.outcome: PPV-sensitivity trade-off
evidence.effect: Serial high-risk ML AND ASQ: PPV 0.050 vs ASQ 0.022, but sensitivity 0.129 vs 0.178.
evidence.quote: Third, serial testing requiring both positive ML classification and positive screening achieved more than a 2-fold improvement in PPV (0.050 vs 0.022) but with reduced sensitivity (0.129 vs 0.178).

evidence.title: External Validation, Recalibration, and Extension of a Prediction Model of Early Acute Kidney Injury in Critically Ill Children Using Multicenter Data
evidence.outcome: Alert burden (PPV and number needed to alert) at chosen cutpoints
evidence.effect: At 90th percentile cutpoint PPV was 10% (PEDSNET-VPS) and 12% (PDC), with NNA 11 and 9; false alerts remain high.
evidence.quote: Future work includes user-focused decision support design based on model results, guided by the need to minimize alert burden given our PPV and NNA results, to improve the actionability and usability of this predictive model ( 48 ).

evidence.title: An interpretable data-driven approach to optimizing clinical fall risk assessment
evidence.outcome: High-risk threshold sensitivity
evidence.effect: At threshold 13, original JHFRAT sensitivity was 0.29 versus augmented CSO 0.57 and XGBoost 0.92.
evidence.quote: The largest performance metric gains are in the sensitivity at the threshold of 13, with the augmented CSO and XGBoost models achieving 0.57 and 0.92 sensitivity compared to the original JHFRAT’s sensitivity of 0.29.

evidence.title: Testing Transferability of a Mortality Risk Model for Interhospital Transfer Using Real-World Electronic Health Records: External Validation and Model Enhancement
evidence.outcome: Precision-recall trade-off implying false-alarm burden at operating threshold
evidence.effect: Recall was at least 0.70 in most configurations but precision remained below 0.70 in several settings, indicating many false positives even in top models.
evidence.quote: However, precision remained less than 0.70 in several settings, reflecting a notable rate of false positives.

evidence.title: Alert Policy and Rare-Event Metrics for Seven-Day-Ahead Agitation Forecasting in Passive Dementia Monitoring
evidence.outcome: caregiver alert precision under default thresholds
evidence.effect: default thresholds yielded 20–23% precision with 94–100% recall, which was unacceptable for caregiver-facing alerts
evidence.quote: Default thresholds yielded 20–23% precision with 94– 100% recall—unacceptable for caregiver-facing alerts.

evidence.title: ImmunoResponse Predictor: a GUI for accurate response prediction to immunotherapy
evidence.outcome: Asymmetric score cutoffs minimizing false negatives across cohorts
evidence.effect: FNR 0% (PCD mUC), 33% (PCD mRCC), 25% (Moreno), 27% (UNC-108); precision 41%, 40%, 100%, 24%.
evidence.quote: The associated false negative rates (FNRs; corresponding precisions) were 0% (41%) for PCD (mUC), 33% (40%) for PCD (mRCC), 25% (100%) for Moreno, and 27% (24%) for UNC-108 (see Table 1 for details).

commentary.bottom_line: Studies of threshold adjustment suggest that cutoffs chosen with response capacity in mind can reduce alert volume without a clear loss of detection, but only one retrospective study tested clinician involvement directly. Certainty is low because most evidence is simulated and no study compared clinician-selected cutoffs with default cutoffs on patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Of 15 studies, one cluster RCT (n=9887) reported a 12% decrease in administered high-risk drug combinations, and two prospective comparisons reported lower alert volume after threshold adjustment. No study compared clinician-selected cutoffs with default cutoffs, and most were simulated. Certainty is therefore low because of indirectness and study design.

Raising cutoffs lowers alert volume but can miss patients. In one simulation, a cutoff of 4 raised estimated sepsis deaths from 9 to 18 cases. In another model, lowering the threshold to 0.33 raised sensitivity from 38.5% to 51.3%, and false positives rose from 119 to 207. These trade-offs suggest that teams need explicit agreement on acceptable misses.

Only one study, from Singapore, set a threshold with physicians and radiologists. In a retrospective replay, that threshold retained 93.19% sensitivity and 35.85% operational improvement. Silent alert simulations across four models supported capacity-aligned thresholds but predicted postimplementation performance poorly. A Korean ward study found that a cutoff of 94 rather than 91 better discriminated physician intervention, which suggests cutoffs may need revision after go-live.

In a screening program of 145,848 patients, adjusting the operating point cut alerts from 4.4% to 2.3%, with no difference in enrolment rate among reviewed alerts. In Hungarian mammography, moving the threshold to match workload capacity reduced flagged cases from 10.6–11.2% to 7.4%, while additional cancer detection stayed at 0.7 per 1,000. One trial of alert follow-up described staff burden as high.

Two tests included rural populations, in Hungary and China. One obstetric replay had a racial and ethnic minority focus, and in that study a 0.2 threshold missed fewer at-risk patients than 0.3. No test reported Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy groups, so it is unknown whether capacity-driven cutoffs shift missed cases toward these patients.

commentary.research_gap: No study randomized or prospectively compared cutoffs selected with clinician input and capacity data against statistically derived or vendor-default cutoffs in live deployment. None measured missed high-risk patients, patient outcomes, and staff workload together over time.
commentary.underserved_note: Three tests included rural populations or had a racial and ethnic minority focus. None included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups should not assume that cutoffs tuned elsewhere will balance missed patients and alert burden the same way for their patients.
